content.title: Profitability is determined before the first ground is broken
content.description: The decisions with the greatest impact on a property's profitability and long-term value are often made before construction begins. Yet many projects focus on construction costs, while fewer focus on decisions affecting the property's operation, flexibility and development potential.
content.extendedDescription:
Building services and energy affect a property throughout its lifetime. They influence how the building is used, managed, adapted and developed.

At Hamnplan 222, we are displaying EkoNod's demonstration module. It offers a practical insight into how building services and energy can be viewed as a system, and how that perspective can influence a project's development.

Visit the module and discuss how earlier decisions can contribute to more profitable properties, lower project risk, greater flexibility over time and higher long-term property value.

content.title: How much treatment can we afford? Finding a shared path to sustainable healthcare
content.description: Primary care should be the hub of Swedish healthcare. Why is this cost-effective as medicine costs and care needs for common conditions such as obesity, diabetes and mental ill-health increase? Other societal measures are also needed for sustainable healthcare. What investments should be made?
content.extendedDescription:
Primary care should be the hub of Swedish healthcare, an excellent and resource-efficient approach from a system-wide perspective. But challenges are numerous, and primary care must take growing responsibility for meeting population needs. Treatable common conditions continue to become more prevalent, including obesity, affecting 18% of the population, diabetes and mental ill-health. Costs to individuals, society and healthcare are rising. Effective help exists, but prioritisation is increasingly difficult.
SFAM, with expertise in general practice and unique insight into the patient population, therefore wants to discuss this with experienced public health and obesity experts from Karolinska Institutet. How do society, economics and health connect, and how can we reason wisely about the way forward?
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: E-cigarettes under scrutiny – from niche product to regulated market: what do we know today?
content.description: E-cigarettes have been available in Sweden for more than 15 years and are now used by hundreds of thousands of adults. Meanwhile, the debate centres on questions about health, product safety, young people's use and strict regulation. What does the market look like today, and what do we really know about the products?
content.extendedDescription:
Over the past fifteen years, e-cigarettes have developed from a niche product into an established and growing part of the Swedish nicotine market. Meanwhile, regulation has become more extensive, with increasing requirements for product safety, ingredient declarations and traceability.

But the debate about e-cigarettes is still marked by many questions. How is e-liquid manufactured? How do today's safety checks work? What does use among adults and young people look like? How does today's market differ from the one that emerged in the 2010s? How does a market function when small local businesses operate alongside multinational giants?

The discussion examines this development from manufacturers', retailers' and consumers' perspectives. It focuses on changes in the market, product safety, quality requirements, common misconceptions about e-cigarettes and the challenges and opportunities ahead.

The aim is to provide a fact-based picture of a product category relevant to both public health and the future of nicotine policy.
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: When protection is not enough – for safety today and less exclusion tomorrow
content.description: How can we create long-term safety after a child has been protected? Stockholm will be the first in Sweden to implement an evidence-based treatment model for families where children have experienced violence or serious neglect.
content.extendedDescription:
How can we create long-term safety after a child has been protected? During the seminar, we discuss how coordinated, evidence-based interventions can increase children's safety, promote healing and create conditions for lasting change in families where violence and neglect have occurred.

Why is Stockholms stad the first municipality in Sweden to invest in MST-CAN? We explore how the model can help break destructive patterns, reduce the need for placements and create better long-term outcomes for children and families – while using society's resources more effectively.

content.title: Does Sweden have racist laws?
content.description: In recent years, Sweden has introduced a series of new laws, reforms and political proposals on migration and integration. On the surface, they may appear neutral and equal for everyone – but are they really?
content.extendedDescription:
We believe the new rules have particularly significant consequences for people of non-European backgrounds and raise questions about fairness, equal treatment and human rights. Sweden has long been seen as a frontrunner in tolerance and the equal worth of all people. At the same time, political developments have moved towards the EU's minimum standards in migration policy.

What does this mean for those affected? How are young people of non-European backgrounds affected in their daily lives, dreams for the future and sense of belonging? Why are these issues so rarely discussed on Almedalsveckan's major stages?

In this discussion, young people from KISAM – Världens ungdomar share their own experiences, stories and perspectives. Their voices offer insight into how today's policies affect individuals and the consequences they may have for Sweden's future.

content.title: Humans as masters of creation or relatives among other beings – different perspectives and consequences?
content.description: How do we experience our relationship with the rest of the planet? Are humans in charge, or are we all equally important and interconnected? What does it mean that our experiences differ? How does Svenska kyrkan view this from biblical and human perspectives? What do the performing arts think, and what do you think?
content.extendedDescription:
A warm welcome to an open public conversation with guests from Visby Stift and the performing arts collective Tellus°. The gathering begins with a special version of Tellus°#3: Sympoiesis, a physical performance that premiered in February at Naturhistoriska Museet in Gothenburg. The performance then transitions into the conversation, both taking place inside Visby Domkyrka.
Tellus°#3: Sympoiesis is a physical, multidisciplinary artwork in which voice, movement, music and video portray humanity's attempt to reconnect with the living world it has never really left. We journey out of the Anthropocene – a popular way of viewing our human-dominated and sometimes ruthless era – and glimpse the Chthulucene, a very different and at least equally true account of our world. Shaped by ancient mechanisms and collaborations between life and matter, constantly evolving symbioses and relationships between life, time and rhythm. Natural laws and phenomena that seem undeterred by restrictive norms, structures and behaviours.

content.title: Thoughts for the day with the Minister for Justice: a freer and safer Sweden
content.description: Freedom and safety are two sides of the same coin. Parents should feel able to let children cycle home alone from football practice, and women should not have to look over their shoulders on the way home. Dangerous criminals should be inside so you feel safe outside.
content.extendedDescription:
This is Moderaterna's safety pledge for the next parliamentary term.

Sweden is on the right path, but has not arrived. Lethal gang violence has more than halved. So have personal robberies against boys under 18 and profits from fraud against older people. Police numbers have increased substantially, more serious crimes are solved and we are regaining control of more residential areas.

At the same time, the work against gangs must be completed. This concerns violence, the criminal economy and recruitment of children. We must also focus on other serious crime, such as men's violence against women, sexual offences and honour-based oppression.

Join breakfast with Gunnar Strömmer to hear his thoughts on safety and freedom in Sweden over the next four years. Above all, this will be an open discussion with plenty of room for your questions.

content.title: Commercialising deep tech – from breakthrough to scalable business
content.description: Sweden has the research, but too many deep tech innovations get stuck between the lab and the market. How do we commercialise what the market does not yet know how to buy, and what is needed for Swedish breakthroughs to become scalable global businesses?
content.extendedDescription:
Circle Series is an initiative within Tech Forward, a collaboration between Techarenan and Teknikföretagen, in which 8–16 hand-picked decision-makers, experts and innovators come together to explore an urgent topic related to innovation, growth and the future in depth.

Unlike traditional panel discussions, Circle Series is an active conversation in which all participants contribute. Each circle has a leader and meets 4–6 times over a year, creating continuity, trust and the opportunity to move from insight to actual action.

The circle on commercialising deep tech starts during Almedalsveckan 2026, meets again in the autumn and concludes at Techarenan's major event in February 2027.

content.title: The distance between life and death — can the industry unite against railway trespassing?
content.description: Every day, rail traffic in Sweden is affected by people on or near the tracks. The consequences can be serious for the individual, the train driver, passengers and the entire railway system.
content.extendedDescription: Railway trespassing causes more than accidents and near misses. It also leads to disruption, delays and reduced punctuality. Every time trains are stopped or slowed down, thousands of passengers and large parts of the transport system are affected. During Almedalsveckan, Järnvägsbranschens samverkansforum (JBS) brings together leading representatives of the railway sector, public transport and politics to discuss why the issue matters so much, why the industry has chosen to act together and how cooperation can improve safety, punctuality and the resilience of the transport system. This spring, the railway industry has, for the first time, united in a joint national campaign against railway trespassing. The campaign highlights how small the distance can be between a risky decision and a life-changing accident, and how small changes in behaviour can make a big difference.

content.title: What is happening to the global playing field?
content.description: Geopolitical tensions, trade conflicts and new balances of power are changing conditions for business, investment and international cooperation. How do global developments affect Sweden and Swedish companies, and what strategic choices are required?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish companies depend heavily on global markets for both sourcing and sales. Geopolitics, trade barriers and increasingly protectionist industrial policies in several markets make it harder to understand the actual business impact and optimise value chains.

In this discussion, Business Sweden's geopolitical advisers meet policy experts from Swedish companies. Global perspectives are combined with a closer look at US and EU industrial policy and its effects on Swedish businesses.

Main questions include:
- Which recent developments are uppermost in Swedish companies' minds?
- Will US trade policy volatility subside?
- How does EU industrial policy affect companies?
- What is the state of US–EU trade relations?
- What opportunities arise amid the current turbulence?
- What should businesses focus on going forward?

content.title: Managing for outcomes in the public sector
content.description: Managing for outcomes means achieving the desired effects in society based on the purpose of the organisation. Today’s management focuses heavily on the outputs of public organisations, while the purpose is lost in practice. Why is this? What can we do instead?
content.extendedDescription:
Welfare services such as healthcare, education and social care, and safe communities, are outcomes we seek to achieve. This is difficult and cannot be managed as though it were simple goods production. Yet today’s management still relies heavily on industrial thinking from the turn of the last century. Managing for outcomes means developing management further, starting from the recognition that reality is complex and that no organisation can create outcomes on its own. Outcomes are the result of co-creation.

Welcome to a discussion about how we can change management in the public sector and achieve greater impact with our shared resources. An exploratory conversation in which we try to avoid simplistic solutions and start from the belief that people mean well.

content.title: Employers’ wish list: perfect, experienced, 23 years old
content.description: There is talk of labour shortages, yet thousands of young people still do not get a chance. Employers say they cannot find the right people. Young people say no one wants to give them a chance. High demands, unrealistic expectations and a reluctance to hire people without experience are creating a divide that threatens the next generation.
content.extendedDescription: How can employers talk about labour shortages while many young people never get their first job? This discussion starts with the growing divide between young people and employers and focuses on how job requirements, expectations and recruitment culture affect the opportunity to enter the labour market, and what it takes to give more people the chance to build experience.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: Educated but not employable — who takes responsibility for the gap?
content.description: Many courses do not lead to jobs, and several junior white-collar roles risk disappearing as AI takes over some tasks. The gap between what education provides and what the labour market actually needs is growing. How should education, employers and social systems change
content.extendedDescription:
AI is changing the labour market, and many traditional entry-level roles are being reshaped. As these roles change, the path to a first job risks narrowing, while many courses do not automatically lead to employment. How do we ensure that education continues to lead to work?

Bliwa invites representatives from education, working life and student organisations to discuss how education and working life need to develop together to help young people enter employment in a rapidly changing economy.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: Can digital tools strengthen the knowledge and language skills of health and social care staff?
content.description: How can digital tools strengthen Swedish health and social care through more efficient working methods, better collaboration and higher quality for decision-makers who want to stay ahead?
content.extendedDescription:
Visible Knowledge and VC-appen address one of the welfare system’s greatest challenges: how to ensure skills, quality and equitable care at a time of staff shortages, growing demands and limited resources. VC-appen is a knowledge platform for Swedish health and social care that can be scaled nationally, developed with professionals and adapted to the realities of municipalities and regions.
With more than 550 instructional videos, 60 practice-focused courses and secure video calls, staff can access the right knowledge at the right moment. This reduces reliance on one-off interventions, strengthens patient safety and frees up staff time.
VC-appen shows how smart digitalisation can become a strategic tool for decision-makers who want to strengthen the supply of skilled staff, develop employees’ language skills, increase equity between municipalities and build more sustainable health and social care — here and now, and for the future.

content.title: Local learning centres — a solution for distance-learning exams in today’s AI world, but who pays?
content.description: In today’s world, with more exams that cannot be taken at home because of AI, exam services at learning centres are increasingly important. There is currently no clear standard or funding model for how this should work. A more standardised approach and a funding model are needed.
content.extendedDescription:
Distance-learning exams pose technical challenges, including requirements for up-to-date software (e.g. Inspera) and a stable internet connection. Problems with cheating have increased significantly, leading to more disciplinary cases and the growing replacement of remote exams with on-campus exams. To minimise cheating and enable everyone in Sweden to pursue further education, local learning centres are needed to offer this service, along with a more standardised approach and funding model. Today, more and more smaller learning centres are starting to turn away students who do not live in the municipality. Students in larger cities are affected, as larger cities often lack learning centres. Isn’t that strange?

The room holds 60 people.

SVT covered the issue during the spring. See the link:
https://www.svt.se/nyheter/lokalt/smaland/studenter-i-klam-nar-fusket-ska-stoppas-tvingas-betala-for-tentor
content.instructions: If you cannot attend in person, you are welcome to join online via Zoom!

content.title: Chess as a tool for inclusion, learning and reintegration into society
content.description: Chess is more than a game — it is an educational and social tool that strengthens people’s abilities and creates new routes into society. How can structured chess initiatives contribute both to better school results and to reintegration after prison?
content.extendedDescription:
This event highlights how chess is used as an educational tool in schools and as a rehabilitative intervention in correctional services and reintegration. Drawing on practical experience, we discuss how the game strengthens concentration, problem-solving, impulse control, responsibility and social skills — abilities that are crucial both for success at school and for breaking destructive patterns in life.

We explore how accessible activities such as chess can contribute to social sustainability, inclusion and prevention, and how collaboration between civil society, schools and correctional services can develop. This social issue concerns how structured chess initiatives can contribute both to better school results and to reintegra…

Held as an open conversation around a chessboard, where visitors can take part, ask questions and discuss with us. No advance registration or preparation is required.

content.title: An alternative delivery model — meeting civilian and military needs in the next generation of icebreakers
content.description: How can we ensure that the government’s investment is enough for two new state icebreakers? The SEK 4.1 billion allocation is intended to replace the remaining Atle-class vessels, but rising costs, new European guidelines and geopolitical developments raise questions about how the forthcoming procurement should be designed.
content.extendedDescription:
Reliable icebreaking capacity is a prerequisite for functioning Swedish supply chains, industrial production and competitiveness. The deteriorating security situation and the growing presence of Russia and China in the Arctic have further increased the importance of icebreakers for defence and preparedness.

After a long procurement process, Sjöfartsverket signed a contract for a new icebreaker during the spring. In parallel, the EU has adopted a maritime industrial strategy to strengthen European manufacturing, and a Swedish-Finnish working group has been appointed to develop a long-term vision for future icebreaking capacity. These initiatives may have a significant impact on the design of the forthcoming procurement.

The seminar centres on two questions:
How can the delivery model be designed to deliver two new state icebreakers on time and within the available budget?
How can the dual-use perspective, meaning both civilian and military needs, be ensured for the next generation of state icebreakers?
speakerTitles: Head of the Military Defence Division and Capability Director
Parliamentary Committee on Transport and Communications

content.title: Who takes responsibility for relatives between cancer care and everyday life?
content.description: When cancer strikes, relatives often take on extensive responsibility for care, coordination and support. Yet they lack coherent and equitable support themselves. How can politics and civil society bridge the gap between cancer care and everyday life for families affected by cancer?
content.extendedDescription:
When cancer becomes part of everyday life, life changes for the whole family. Relatives are often expected to coordinate healthcare contacts, provide emotional support and at the same time keep up with work, finances and caring for children. Despite their crucial role in the care pathway, long-term and equitable support structures are often lacking. The association Kraftens hus, which has emerged in several places across the country, offers support both to relatives and to people who have cancer themselves. The question is how responsibility is shared between central government, regions and municipalities — and how civil society can be part of the solution without replacing public responsibility. Needs are increasing as more people live longer with or after cancer.

The event takes the form of a panel discussion bringing different perspectives together with relatives’ experiences. It focuses on how we can create more coherent and sustainable support structures for those affected by cancer.

Also broadcast online.
speakerTitles: Professor of nursing science at Marie Cederschiöld högskola and scientific director of Palliativt kunskapscentrum Region Stockholm

content.title: Does Sweden need a tech minister?
content.description: The Swedish tech success story is entering a new phase as AI companies reach billion-level valuations. The industry is calling for faster reforms, a better supply of skills, simpler regulations and more capital. What are politicians doing to ensure that Sweden does not lose its leading position as a tech nation?
content.extendedDescription:
Dagens industri’s live podcast Technokratin broadcasts from Almedalen. Henrik Ek and his guests discuss the role of tech companies in Swedish business and how politics affects it.
Immediately after the regular broadcast, Boost.ai offers an insight into how AI agents are set to fundamentally change our digital habits. How is a brand affected when users start talking directly to AI agents instead of handling their business on a company’s or public authority’s own website? We explore how companies and public authorities need to rethink their approach as users start delegating tasks to smart digital assistants. How does this affect the relationship between organisations and citizens — and what does it take to keep up with developments?

content.title: When people make a place their own, it becomes safer
content.description: What happens when we let people make use of spaces that are empty and feel unsafe? How can collaboration between property owners, municipalities and civil society turn empty spaces into safe, lively environments in outer-city neighbourhoods?
content.extendedDescription:
When Hemsö took over Campus Tensta in 2022, it found two empty buildings and a place that felt unsafe and abandoned. To help realise Hemsö’s vision of filling the place with life, engagement and hope for the future, a dialogue began with Stockholms stad, local stakeholders and civil society.
Four years later, dialogue has turned into action. The first students at Järva gymnasium have graduated, Tekniska museet has celebrated its first anniversary, and Campus Tensta is now an open, safe and lively meeting place.
In this seminar, several stakeholders share how the place has developed, the challenges along the way and the lessons that can be applied to create safety, a sense of well-being and hope for the future in more places.
speakerTitles: Vice mayor for social affairs and public safety
Chair of the municipal executive board

content.title: Art or expense — what is its value to a place?
content.description: Is public art an expense or an investment? In an open conversation centred on learning, we explore how art and culture affect places and people. What do research and practice tell us — and how can art and culture make a place more attractive and safer, and give it an identity?
content.extendedDescription:
Public art stirs emotions, questions and sometimes opposition. Is it an expense that can be deprioritised — or an investment that creates value beyond what can be measured? Research shows that people feel better in thoughtfully designed environments — but how can that knowledge be put into practice? In this seminar, we invite you to a constructive conversation about what public art and culture actually contribute to a place and the people who live there.

With real-world examples and different perspectives in the room, we discuss the role of art in place development and why property owners, municipalities and other stakeholders need to take responsibility for more than the building itself. Hemsö sees the seminar as an opportunity to develop new insights into how art and culture can become a natural part of strategic work to give a place an identity.
speakerTitles: Municipal commissioner for culture and leisure

content.description: Financial and organised crime are becoming increasingly sophisticated. What does it take for society to withstand the threat to democracy and the rule of law?
content.extendedDescription:
The government promised to prioritise crimes against business owners during its term in office, but after four years all the money seems to have gone towards tackling gang crime. At the same time, we see intimidation methods commonly used in gang crime now also affecting business owners.

Lasse Wierup and Susanna Hestréus and their guests describe how the black market infiltrates both businesses and the public sector, and the consequences for society.

content.title: Veterinary care prices — sustainable animal ownership for the future
content.description: High veterinary care prices can affect animal welfare, food production and public health. How can the sector jointly identify future challenges and develop long-term, practical solutions for accessible and sustainable veterinary care?
content.extendedDescription:
The event brings together a broad panel of leading Swedish expertise in the field. Participants include representatives of insurance companies, veterinarians, politicians, animal owners and other stakeholders. Perspectives from across the entire chain provide a comprehensive picture of how price developments affect animal welfare, access to care and public health.

Vetpris works for greater transparency in veterinary care, but recognises that the market also needs political initiatives to make sustainable long-term solutions possible. The discussion focuses on shared challenges, the division of responsibilities and practical ways forward. The panel discussion lasts approximately two hours and aims to provide a constructive, solution-focused dialogue.

content.title: How do we create lasting solutions for mental and physical health in society?
content.description: Mental and physical ill health is increasing in society, while many interventions only begin once problems have already become extensive. Stress, a lack of recovery and prolonged strain affect both children and adults, leading to higher costs for society and human suffering.
content.extendedDescription:
The event takes as its starting point the increase in mental and physical ill health in society.
We highlight how stress, a lack of recovery and insufficient early intervention affect individuals, families and social structures, and the opportunities for a stronger focus on promoting health.

Through dialogue, we explore different perspectives on how a holistic approach, collaboration and alternative ways of working can improve well-being for both children and adults. The event has an open and welcoming format that allows reflection, the exchange of experiences and shared learning.

content.title: Sustainable health — a possibility or a utopia?
content.description: The need to transition to a sustainable society is becoming increasingly clear as climate change intensifies and biodiversity declines. At the same time, human health and well-being rely heavily on the overuse of natural resources. How can we navigate this conflict between goals?
content.extendedDescription: Welcome to a conversation about the conflict between human health and its dependence on access to fossil energy and natural resources. Can we draw a line for what is “good enough” when it comes to people’s health? Do we need to move to a model in which sufficiency is the guiding principle, or must we continue striving for “the best possible health for all” to meet the challenges facing humanity? How do we combine cutting-edge medical research with fundamental human rights when resources are finite? How do we combine and prioritise the health of the planet in relation to societal development? How can we find a way forward together?

content.title: Media support fit for our times?
content.description: The new media support scheme was introduced in 2024, but expires in just three years. What do politicians want from 2030? Free newspapers became eligible last time — will magazines be included in the system next time? And will there be zero VAT, as in Denmark and Norway?
content.extendedDescription: Will the participating Members of Parliament work towards targeted support for magazines after the election? Today, most magazines are outside the current media support scheme, despite playing a central role in deepening knowledge and providing informed coverage of society. Are they prepared to adjust the definition of a “general news medium” so that, from 2030, a shared system includes daily newspapers, magazines and free newspapers that meet this vital social need in a broad sense? And could zero VAT for newspapers and magazines be introduced as a complement to targeted media support? This would be a simple and predictable model that strengthens the sector’s own capacity and reduces dependence on direct support, which in itself is positive from both a market and a legitimacy perspective.
content.subject: Media/journalism

content.title: How well are freedom of the press and freedom of expression holding up in Sweden?
content.description: Sweden has fallen in international rankings of freedom of the press and freedom of expression. One explanation is restrictions introduced in legislation, but also changes to how courts and public authorities apply the principle of public access to official documents and to their policies on it. How do we reverse this?
content.extendedDescription:
Peter Danowsky began in 1976 as an associate lawyer with press freedom lawyer Göran Luterkort, and in 1993 he co-founded Danowsky & Partners. In 2017, Peter Danowsky received Advokatsamfundet’s award for outstanding contributions, and today he is regarded as one of Sweden’s leading press freedom lawyers. Here, Peter Danowsky, who worked with Bo Strömstedt for many years and has often represented Expressen and other media companies, talks to Thomas Mattsson about the development of free expression in Sweden.

The principle of public access to official documents? Defamation cases? Conflicts of interest? Is it right for lawyers sometimes to represent publishers and sometimes those suing the media? Are the damages awarded reasonable? What does Peter Danowsky think?

In 2007, Peter Danowsky wrote “En resonerande ordbok om tryck- och yttrandefrihet” (TU); in 2012, “Advokatyrket, upphovsrätten och yttrandefriheten” (Norstedts Juridik) was published; and in 2025 he published “Slutplädering – inblick i rättssalen” (Ekerlids förlag).

content.title: Digital sovereignty — from concern to opportunity
content.description: Digital sovereignty is a cornerstone of Sweden’s resilience. AI has moved from a technology issue to a matter of national competitiveness and resilience. Almost 70 per cent of the world’s leading AI models come from the US or China. Control over data, models and infrastructure is now crucial.
content.extendedDescription:
There is broad agreement that Sweden must reconcile sovereignty and innovation rather than choose one over the other. A hybrid strategy is the key, not an all-or-nothing approach. Sweden has an excellent foundation to build on: high digital maturity, stable and green energy, strong technical expertise and a tradition of innovation.

The ambition should be to move from an already strong position to world leadership in applying AI. Sovereign AI is not about isolation. No single actor can solve this alone. Collaboration between politics, business, the public sector and academia is the engine that can give Sweden the economies of scale it needs. Today, few Swedish organisations see sovereign AI as a competitive advantage; most view it solely as risk management. That perspective must change. Sovereign platforms enable secure data sharing, locally adapted models and entirely new business models. Control over AI needs to become a matter for CEOs and boards.

One of the most important prerequisites for good, safe care is staff well-being. Introducing an evidence-based method for well-being would benefit healthcare staff, patients and society as a whole.
content.extendedDescription: Förenade Reikiförbundet i Sverige works to have Reiki included as a complement to health and social care in Sweden. Reiki is a touch-based method from Japan with a long tradition in Eastern medicine. Reiki has gained considerable ground in the West as a complement to healthcare in many other countries. It helps the body activate the recipient’s capacity for self-healing, reducing stress, relieving pain, increasing well-being and accelerating healing. Reiki is currently used in healthcare in countries including England, the US and Australia. There is extensive research on Reiki, but not yet in Sweden. Research has shown positive results in connection with, for example, heart problems, cancer, stress and pain relief. Today, Reiki is approved as a wellness activity in Sweden, and we now want to take the step towards becoming a complement to health and social care.

content.title: Expensive miracles — how do we share the costs of future medicines?
content.description: New cell and gene therapies can cure serious diseases, but cost tens of millions per patient. How should society fund these breakthrough treatments, what should the models for introducing them look like, and how do we ensure equitable access?
content.extendedDescription:
Cell and gene therapies, known as ATMP medicines, offer hope of a cure for patients with serious or rare diseases. A single treatment can, for example, cure haemophilia, but costs more than SEK 30 million. The high one-off costs challenge current funding systems. Even if the effect is long-lasting, there is considerable uncertainty about long-term outcomes. This raises questions about how society should prioritise and pay for these treatments.
Should the cost be spread over time or linked to treatment outcomes? Is there public-sector capital that could be used effectively here? How can equitable access across regions be ensured? Which health economic models are reasonable, and how are benefits for patients and society measured?
The healthcare of the future faces difficult trade-offs between innovation, economics and fairness.

content.title: Air medical services in a new security landscape — how do we strengthen Sweden’s resilience?
content.description: Sweden faces a new security landscape in which hybrid interference, pressure on critical infrastructure and greater vulnerability in essential services require a more coordinated and robust response. As demands on national preparedness grow, resources need to be coordinated more strategically.
content.extendedDescription:
The joint municipal authorities Svenskt ambulansflyg (KSA) and Svensk luftambulans (SLA) invite operational representatives, responsible politicians and officials from the organisations concerned to a panel discussion.
Air medical resources — ambulance aircraft and helicopters — are central to the country’s ability to provide advanced care quickly and carry out life-saving transport over long distances.
How do we ensure sustained operations during disruptions? How do we create redundancy? And how should responsibility and collaboration between public authorities and other actors develop?
In this panel discussion, we want to explore the decisions and structures that may be needed to strengthen Sweden’s overall resilience — in peacetime, crisis and war.

content.title: Are we strong enough to cope with war?
content.description: The uncertain international situation is prompting Sweden to rearm. Defence is receiving more resources and industry’s order books are full. But what about the population — are we physically fit enough to cope with a war?
content.extendedDescription:
Increasing rates of overweight and poorer health habits pose a problem for our preparedness. If we lack the capacity to carry out the tasks required in war, whether military or civilian, we become vulnerable. What can politicians do to strengthen the Swedish population’s physical capability? How can the gym and fitness industry help the whole population exercise more? Are there forms of exercise or particular activities that are especially important if we are to cope with war?
Welcome to Opinionstältet in Almedalen to hear experts and industry representatives discuss our physical preparedness.

content.title: The public sector secures data centres but overlooks threats from its own computers
content.description: The public sector places great emphasis on cybersecurity, data storage and control over sensitive information. But what risks arise from its own IT equipment? How do we ensure that devices do not pose a security risk throughout their lifecycle, from purchasing and use to take-back, erasure and decommissioning?
content.extendedDescription:
All too often, devices are left in storerooms, cupboards and drawers without clear responsibility, traceability or secure erasure.
In this panel discussion, 3stepIT brings together representatives from the public sector, cybersecurity and procurement to discuss how public organisations can manage IT equipment securely, cost-effectively and sustainably.

content.title: Sweden can lead the adoption of breakthrough technologies and AI in healthcare
content.description: How can Sweden address the complex challenges facing healthcare and enable precision medicine by combining patient data, AI, technology development and research?
content.extendedDescription: Sweden has unique strengths: world-leading university hospitals, reliable health data, SciLifeLab’s national research infrastructure, high-quality research and advanced technology development at universities. Systematically connecting university research, SciLifeLab’s research infrastructure and university hospitals enables faster adoption of advanced technology for clinical benefit. Joint units at university hospitals can develop and adapt advanced technologies in molecular analysis, data-driven research and AI to strengthen clinical research and the widespread implementation of precision medicine in Sweden. Long-term funding for these units and collaboration between healthcare, academia, industry and patients are crucial to achieving this ambitious but necessary goal. We discuss why these joint structures need to be created and how they can be designed to strengthen Sweden’s research close to clinical practice.

content.title: Procuring HR and payroll systems for the future
content.description: We live in a time when society and technology are developing rapidly. With AI, we can now accomplish things in entirely new ways. How can we future-proof procurement of payroll and HR systems, with contracts that may run for 10–20 years, when we do not know what will happen next week?
content.extendedDescription:
In procurement, it is common to specify requirements based on today’s circumstances and systems. This is natural and understandable, as it reflects actual experience and frames of reference. But taking a step back, the requirements for “today’s” systems and solutions may have been set 10 years ago, and there is an obvious risk of ending up in a “parade of history”. How should we think and act to meet tomorrow’s requirements? Future-proofing an organisation is crucial to creating good conditions for employees, pupils, care recipients and citizens.
How can smarter procurement of payroll and HR systems create opportunities for development? What are the implications for the choice of procurement procedure, the management of requirements, supplier evaluation or the choice of system architecture? Above all, this is about people — how do we bring employees with us?
“Everyone wants progress, but no one wants change.” — Søren Aabye Kierkegaard.

HR strategist and HR systems management lead

content.title: Stop misogyny — in memory of Ing-Marie Wieselgren
content.description: Women are never free from men’s hatred and violence. Women are not safe at home, on streets or in public squares, or when they participate in democratic debate. In 2022, Ing-Marie Wieselgren was brutally murdered by a man whose sole aim was to come to Almedalen and silence a woman in the debate.
content.extendedDescription:
For the fourth year running, the Stoppa kvinnohatet rally is being held in memory of Ing-Marie Wieselgren. The murder of Ing-Marie Wieselgren in Almedalen in 2022 was a brutal attack not only on an individual woman, but on open debate and our democracy. When women are silenced, restricted or withdraw from public life, the whole of society is weakened.

Stopping men’s violence and misogyny requires both urgent action and long-term work for gender equality, safety and inclusive democratic debate.

The rally brings together actors from civil society, politics and other parts of society to jointly draw attention to and counter violence, threats and hatred against women, and to defend everyone’s right to participate in public debate.

Achieving real change is a shared responsibility, in which prevention, protection and a strong commitment to democracy go hand in hand.
speakerTitles: Family and gender equality policy spokesperson
Member of Parliament, Parliamentary Committee on Health and Welfare

content.title: How can we build voluntary bridges between people through shared interests?
content.description: We see gaps opening up between generations, cultures, socioeconomic groups and life experiences. These distances risk leading to mistrust, polarisation and reduced social cohesion. When people do not meet, trust weakens. How people build bridges through a shared interest.
content.extendedDescription:
15 minutes of information, followed by an open conversation in the Hot Seat, centred on reflection, dialogue and listening together. No preparation is required — come as you are, with your curiosity and experiences. During this session, we also explain what Bbeabridge has done over the years and what we do today to create meeting places, strengthen community and contribute to a more inclusive society.

The social issue we want to explore is growing exclusion and the gaps that emerge between people in society — between generations, cultures, socioeconomic groups and different life experiences. We see how the lack of natural meeting places leads to reduced trust, increased polarisation and a sense of loneliness, even though we live in a constantly connected society.

The problem is not only economic or structural; it is also relational. Life has meaning, and we can all build bridges and create peace together. Author Fatima Essaidi is a guest.
content.instructions: You are welcome to join in and listen if you would like to ask questions or take part in the Q&A after the 15 minutes in the Hot Seat.

content.title: How strong is the safety net when healthcare makes mistakes?
content.description: When serious mistakes occur in healthcare, the entire safety net around the patient is put to the test. Every year, more than 20 000 care-related injuries are reported that are serious enough to become a matter of compensation. But ensuring that healthcare learns from mistakes is just as important as compensation. How do we get better at that?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has established systems and procedures for what to do when a care-related injury occurs. Yet mistakes and accidents raise many questions about responsibility and transparency. Responsibility is clear in theory, but what happens in practice when it comes to feedback and action to prevent mistakes from recurring?
* How are patients, relatives and staff given information and support when something has gone wrong, and how can openness and dialogue help prevent mistakes from recurring?
* How do we enable learning from mistakes in healthcare?
* What structures and cultures are needed for healthcare to benefit from experience, change routines and prevent future errors?
speakerTitles: Chief medical officer, chair of the national collaboration group for patient safety

content.title: Pursuing journalists and evasive people in power — how can we meet halfway?
content.description: The greatest obstacle to investigative journalism is not a lack of tips, but people feeling that contributing is too risky, too complicated or pointless. How do we build courage, a sense of safety and trust in investigative journalism?
content.extendedDescription:
When people stop talking, it becomes harder to scrutinise power, wrongdoing and corruption. Journalists report that fewer people are willing to provide tips, give interviews or speak publicly for fear of threats, public pile-ons or consequences at work. Meanwhile, important stories risk never being heard.

What happens to society when silence spreads? And what will it take to restore trust in public debate?
content.subject: Media/journalism

content.title: Climate declarations in 2028 — what happens when building installation work is included?
content.description: From January 2028, under a proposal from Boverket, the legal requirement to calculate the climate impact of new construction will also cover materials and installation work. Knowledge of materials, climate data and installation methods with a lower climate impact will be crucial. Projects being completed in 2028 are being designed now — it is time to act!
content.extendedDescription:
By January 2028 at the latest, under a proposal from Boverket, flooring installation work will also be covered by the legal requirement for climate declarations for new construction. This means that the climate impact of not only materials but also their installation must be calculated and reported. For the construction and property sector, this brings new demands for knowledge, data, allocation of responsibilities and collaboration throughout the value chain, from design to completed building.

The panel discussions bring together representatives of construction companies, nationwide builders, property managers, architects, material suppliers and contractors to discuss what the change means in practice. The focus is on how the industry can prepare for 2028, which challenges need to be addressed and how today’s projects are affected by tomorrow’s regulations.
content.subject: Construction

content.title: How can music, art, culture and role models build bridges across exclusion?
content.description: Around 700 000 people in Sweden live in social isolation. Culture is not just entertainment — it is belonging. When people create, share and experience culture together, a sense of community emerges beyond background, finances and language. Shared interests build natural bridges. How do we create bridges?
content.extendedDescription:
In this session, Bbeabridge shows how we use and have used culture in a wide variety of ways. We also share stories of how we created the peace song Ingen Fara with Dagny Carlsson. How we got school pupils interested in history and made a film together. We explain what we do and what others can learn from our cultural work. We also describe how we build bridges through culture to other countries by creating common ground and a sense of safety. We have experienced how art heals and builds bridges; Dagny Carlsson and Bbeabridge visited different places and painted mandalas. Marianne Hiort af Ornäs will say more about how art builds bridges from the inside out.

Creative expression opens doors where words are not enough.

Cultural activities create safe spaces for new relationships.

Creating together strengthens identity and self-esteem.

Culture provides an accessible first bridge into society.

Ingela Karlsson, theatre educator, director and scriptwriter, takes part in a dialogue with an artist.

content.title: How can we reduce polarisation, trust and people’s growing sense of exclusion?
content.description: The distance between people is growing — a gap expressed through greater polarisation, reduced trust and a growing sense of exclusion. Despite technological progress and constant connectivity, many experience loneliness and a lack of belonging. How can we reduce the gap between people?
content.extendedDescription:
Building interest and bridges to knowledge through empathy. A person needs to be seen as a star, not as a problem. A conversation about bridges between individuals and knowledge that strengthen self-esteem and a sense of direction.

Focus in the Hot Seat:
How empathy can be a practical tool
Awakening curiosity and hope for the future
Building interest that leads to personal development
How we recognise people’s potential rather than their shortcomings

Message: empathy is the starting point for change.
The audience is invited to discuss: how can empathy become a structural force, rather than just an individual quality?

The problem is not only economic or structural — it is also relational. When people do not meet in meaningful settings, we risk losing both social cohesion and hope for the future. Many people have ideas, commitment and a desire to contribute, but without platforms where they can be seen and collaborate, even the best idea is powerless. Social sustainability requires active bridge-building. Welcoming guests.

content.title: Walking across borders — shared walks in Sweden, Spain and France can reduce isolation
content.description: Group walks can reduce feelings of loneliness and create new relationships. Moving together at a gentle pace often makes it easier to share thoughts than sitting opposite one another. When people also leave their home environment — for example through walks in European countries.
content.extendedDescription:
We highlight nature as common ground and walking as a way of getting people moving, both physically and mentally. When people walk side by side in nature, a different kind of encounter emerges. Conversations can develop organically and without pressure to perform. Nature creates calm, presence and space for reflection, strengthening both well-being and mental clarity.

In nature, we remember who we are beyond roles, demands and noise. We hold and lift one another. Mother Earth, our strength from the heart and body. Mother Earth is us, you, you, all of you and me.

Travelling in a safe group opens up new perspectives. Meeting in a new environment: Ingela Karlsson is familiar with theatre, scriptwriting, directing and walking in France in the footsteps of Jeanne d`Arc.

We therefore want to highlight how nature and shared walks can become an important meeting place. In our conversation, we discuss organised trips to Santiago de Compostela and other walks. Important conversations often happen in natural surroundings.

content.title: Cancer cases are increasing — can Sweden afford to rely on the old system?
content.description: More effective cancer treatments mean more patients are living longer with cancer. Pressure on cancer care is increasing, and hospitals cannot keep up. Although care outside hospitals has been shown to halve costs and improve patient benefits, rigid regulations and funding models are slowing the transition
content.extendedDescription:
The new cancer strategy sets the direction for the next 10–15 years and emphasises the need to balance highly specialised hospital care with more decentralised, person-centred treatment.
Akademiska sjukhuset’s Gränbyprojekt and Cancervård nära dig in Uppsala show how parts of specialist care can be moved to smaller clinics, halving the cost per treatment and giving patients better access and shorter journeys. Despite clear benefits for both patients and healthcare economics, structures for scaling up the model are lacking because current reimbursement systems favour traditional hospital care. To ensure that the strategy goes beyond words, new, sustainable structures that facilitate decentralisation are needed.
Welcome to a seminar where decision-makers, experts and patients discuss how we can move from pilot projects to a national standard for the cancer care of the future.

content.title: Sweden at a crossroads: faster introduction of cancer medicines for greater competitiveness
content.description: Despite an ambitious national cancer strategy, it still takes far too long for new, innovative cancer medicines to reach patients. Differences in implementation between regions lead to unequal care and direct consequences for survival and quality of life.
content.extendedDescription:
On the Vårdarenan stage, we bring together some of Sweden’s key actors in cancer care to discuss how to shorten the path from a decision to actual treatment. The starting point is patients’ needs, but also what slow and unpredictable implementation means for the system’s legitimacy and Sweden’s position as a leading life science nation.
The discussion focuses on three crucial questions:
* How can follow-up and the use of national knowledge support be strengthened to enable truly equitable cancer care?
* What is needed for new cancer medicines to reach patients faster, particularly where time literally saves lives?
* How can more predictable and faster implementation strengthen Sweden’s competitiveness, make it more attractive for clinical trials and promote investment?
A conversation for politicians, decision-makers, healthcare professionals, patient representatives and others who want to contribute to world-class cancer care, where patient benefits and future competitiveness go hand in hand.

content.title: Techno-existence: shaping an existentially sustainable future with advanced AI technology
content.description: The rapid development of AI offers many new opportunities, but also raises major and complex questions for our time, with practical relevance for many individuals now and long-term implications for society.
content.extendedDescription:
Rapid digital development receives extensive media coverage and generates substantial research, increasingly including new perspectives from the humanities and social sciences.
This seminar starts from ongoing research and collaborative initiatives at Uppsala universitet. The conversation explores the possibilities and limitations of advanced technology, drawing on the questions these projects address.
Among other things, we consider existential questions at the intersection of disability and technology. We also address dilemmas arising from the increasing use of AI tools in the exercise of public authority.

Using well-known, current examples relevant to our theme, researchers from different disciplines talk with representatives of parties affected by these issues. What does it mean to be human in a time of dramatic technological development? Which norms of what it means to be human are reproduced through AI, and which new norms are reinforced? And which ways of being are made possible or impossible by technological development?
speakerTitles: Senior lecturer in museum and heritage studies
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Without industrial skills, total defence collapses
content.description: Industry’s ability to keep production running is crucial to strong total defence. But in war, conditions change rapidly as the need for production and management skills grows. Do we have the right conditions today to ensure industrial resilience when it really matters?
content.extendedDescription:
Resilience is about military capability, but lessons from Ukraine show that it is also about keeping industrial production running. Factories, workshops and control rooms must remain staffed to maintain society’s functioning beyond the front line and keep production going for society and defence.

After the pandemic, many people came to believe that industry’s role in a crisis was primarily to start making something different. In reality, industry needs to keep doing what it already does in a crisis or war, so that production continues.

At the same time, conditions change when employees are called up for other parts of total defence. Organisations must deliver with fewer resources, making the right skills in both production and management crucial to maintaining industry’s contribution to total defence. How can cooperation between politics, the education system and business ensure that total defence is sustained?

content.title: The technology race is being decided now — how Sweden can keep up
content.description: The US, China and emerging economies are investing heavily in cutting-edge technology and technical talent. Sweden’s competitiveness and prosperity are now being challenged in ways and at a speed we have never experienced before. To secure our leading position in the global technology race, Sweden needs to establish a technology council.
content.extendedDescription:
At the end of March, Trump presented the President’s Council on Science and Technology. It includes world-leading companies in software, hardware, quantum technology, nuclear power and fusion power, and will help the president make strategic decisions on new technologies. The council is led by the former White House Chief Technology Officer, a role established by Obama back in 2009.

But the US is not alone in having this kind of advisory function close to the country’s highest political leadership. It also exists in Japan, South Korea, the UK and other countries.

One country that lacks a technology council, however, is Sweden. Our high-tech industry has long enabled us to maintain a leading global position. But the situation today is very different from just ten years ago. Around the world, countries are investing heavily in cutting-edge technology and technical talent. Our technical expertise and competitiveness are now being challenged in unprecedented ways. The government that takes office after the election needs a technology council.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Dependence on fossil fuels increases our vulnerability
content.description: Geopolitical conflicts can quickly affect our energy prices. How can reduced dependence on fossil fuels strengthen Europe’s economy, security and climate?
content.extendedDescription:
Europe faces a new strategic landscape in which geopolitical uncertainty and vulnerable value chains force difficult choices. In this situation, the pace of the climate transition is increasingly questioned, but for Sweden’s technology industry, the conclusion is not that we should slow the transition — quite the opposite. Ambitious climate policy is our most important tool for strengthening Europe’s competitiveness and strategic autonomy.
Breaking dependence on fossil fuels is not only about cutting emissions; it is about resilience. Electrification, the circular economy and digitalisation make us less vulnerable to geopolitical uncertainty and create new markets for innovation. But investment requires stable rules. Lowering ambitions risks undermining security of supply and technological leadership.
How do we ensure that Sweden and the EU stay on course? Welcome to a conversation about using climate and environmental policy to strengthen industry, secure jobs and build a safer Europe.
speakerTitles: Minister for Climate and the Environment

content.description: A strong industry makes Sweden resilient, secure and sustainable — so how do we keep building the world’s best industry?
content.extendedDescription:

Sweden’s five leading industrial organisations bring politics and business together to discuss industry’s conditions, now and in the future.

content.title: Should children’s right to both parents depend on whether their parents are married?
content.description: Chapter 6, Section 3 of the Parental Code still means that children of unmarried parents are not under joint custody from birth. What are the legal, practical and human consequences for children, parents and confidence in family law?
content.extendedDescription:
The conversation starts from a fundamental question: why should a child’s legal starting point depend on whether their parents are married at birth? We explore how the current provisions in Chapter 6, Section 3 of the Parental Code affect children’s contact with both parents, the balance of power between parents and the view of equal parenthood in Swedish law. We also discuss whether the legislation is compatible with modern family forms and the principle of the child’s best interests.

Please read Chapter 6, Section 3 of the Parental Code before the seminar:
“From birth, the child is in the custody of both parents if they are married to each other, and otherwise in the sole custody of the mother.”

content.title: Bostadsboken — innovative digitalisation of the planning and development process together with users
content.description: The housing shortage has knock-on effects that slow growth, hinder recruitment and undermine the conditions for a vibrant countryside. It is a complex reality in which facts and political priorities do not always point in the same direction. Better knowledge is a prerequisite for sound decisions.
content.extendedDescription:
During Almedalsveckan 2025, Region Gotland launched Bostadsboken, an interactive mapping tool that visualises statistics, facts, opportunities and obstacles for Gotland’s future development. The tool quickly attracted considerable interest among political decision-makers, entrepreneurs and Gotland residents, and received Region Gotland’s Förnyelsepris 2025.

A year has now passed. Bostadsboken has grown through close dialogue with users and partners and now covers more than housing: business, local services and children’s journeys to school are also included. Balancing housing development with the development of business and public services is important. We must build a sustainable society, not just housing.

The seminar presents the parts of Bostadsboken that have attracted the most interest and been most useful, followed by a panel discussion from users’ perspectives. What happens when facts meet reality? And what is needed beyond a good tool to actually bring about change?

content.title: Why do older people fall? How can data help us understand and prevent falls?
content.description: Falls are one of the most common causes of injury among older people — but what causes them? How can systematic fall analysis provide entirely new insights and strengthen prevention in elderly care?
content.extendedDescription:
Falls among older people are a growing social problem affecting quality of life, safety and resources in health and social care. Although many services actively assess risks and take measures to improve safety, they often lack a comprehensive picture of what actually causes falls and which patterns can be changed.
In this seminar, we take a closer look at how fall analysis can provide practical support in everyday work, in residential care and home care. We show how service data can be used to understand connections, identify trends and target interventions where they are most useful.
Together with the audience, we discuss:
• What causes falls in residential care, and why do certain patterns recur?
• How can fall analysis strengthen quality improvement and increase safety for both residents and staff?
The session draws on real examples from Swedish elderly care, focusing on learning, co-creation and benefits for society.

content.title: Warning signs of corruption are increasing — why do we act only when the crisis arrives?
content.description: Corruption, improper influence and organised crime — how do we spot the signs before trust is damaged?
content.extendedDescription:
Corruption rarely looks like it does in the movies. It often begins much more quietly.

A relationship that becomes too close. A lunch that passes unnoticed. Improper influence that no one really wants to talk about. A missed signal. A culture where no one dares to speak up.

By the time wrongdoing is discovered, the damage is often already extensive — financially, organisationally and in terms of trust. Meanwhile, the risks in Sweden are growing. Improper influence, insider threats, organised crime and infiltration are testing both the public and private sectors.

So why do we not spot the signs earlier? Are the obstacles cultural or organisational, or is responsibility unclear?

This seminar brings together some of Sweden’s most interesting voices in anti-corruption, whistleblowing, intelligence work and risk management that upholds legal safeguards, to discuss how organisations can take a more preventive approach, detect more problems in time and act before a crisis is a reality.
speakerTitles: Coordinator against welfare crime and improper influence
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.title: Artificial Intelligence, Democracy, and the 2026 Swedish Elections
content.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to make elections more efficient, inclusive, and secure, but also to disrupt democratic and electoral processes. With the Swedish general elections scheduled for September 2026, understanding how AI affects elections in the Swedish context is critical.
content.extendedDescription:
Are we prepared for elections in the AI era? How do we make the best use of AI for our democracies?

Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to make elections more efficient, inclusive, and secure, but also to disrupt democratic and electoral processes. With the Swedish general elections scheduled for September 2026, understanding how AI affects elections in the Swedish context is critical.

In this Almedalen seminar, International IDEA, the Swedish Election Authority, and Microsoft bring together global, national, and technological perspectives on elections, AI, and democracy. The Swedish Election Authority will provide a national perspective on how Sweden is addressing the challenges posed by AI while exploring its potential to strengthen electoral processes. Microsoft contributes to the discussion from the forefront of AI development, and International IDEA shares examples and best practices from working with electoral authorities globally.

content.title: Children’s voices in custody disputes — what is needed for children to be heard in their own words?
content.description: Children have the right to be heard under the Convention on the Rights of the Child. Custody disputes require interviews with children that uphold legal safeguards, for example through recordings, so that children’s own words reach the court. Sweden should strengthen protection against parental alienation and give children the right to complain directly to the UN.
content.extendedDescription:
Under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, children have the right to be heard on matters affecting them. In custody disputes, it is crucial that children’s own words — not their parents’ interpretations — reach the court. Interviews with children therefore need documentation that upholds legal safeguards, for example through audio or video recording. Sweden should also ratify the Convention’s third Optional Protocol so that children can complain directly to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child.

Children subjected to psychological influence or parental alienation may find it difficult to express their own free will, requiring specialist expertise and protected settings for interviews. Denmark has already introduced parental alienation as a legal concept, while Sweden lacks clear regulation. The case law of the European Court of Human Rights shows that states can be held responsible if they fail to protect the relationship between a child and a parent.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Who will build the companies of the future? Women’s entrepreneurship and mental health
content.description: Sweden needs more entrepreneurs who contribute innovation and new perspectives to growth across the country. Yet we risk missing out on considerable growth potential: young women who want and are able to start businesses. Can entrepreneurship in school help bring about change, and if so, how?
content.extendedDescription: Sweden ranks near the bottom of EU countries for women’s entrepreneurship. This is not about a lack of ambition or ideas, but structural barriers such as limited access to capital, fewer networks, a lack of role models and norms that affect both opportunities and self-image. Yet we see a different picture in schools. In UF student enterprises, where upper-secondary pupils run a business for one school year, participation is almost evenly split between girls and boys. UF entrepreneurship gives young people the courage to test ideas, the safety to fail without risk and knowledge of finance, business and networking — factors often identified as barriers to women’s entrepreneurship. Led by UF alumni and the founders of Ångestpodden together with guests, the conversation explores how mental health and social structures affect young people’s choices. It highlights how early experience and the right support can determine who gets the opportunity to build the companies of the future. The conversation is recorded in front of an audience.
content.subject: Gender equality

content.title: From STEM to STEAM — why Sweden’s innovation policy needs the arts
content.description: Sweden has built its competitiveness on strong STEM skills. But when innovation needs to address complex social challenges and rapid change, the question goes beyond science and technology. Who imagines the futures we should aim for? And who understands the people the technology is designed for?
content.extendedDescription:
Anna Valtonen, Vice-chancellor of Konstfack, and Martin Nilsson Jacobi, Vice-chancellor of Chalmers, meet for an in-depth conversation. As members of the government’s STEM delegation, they discuss how a clearer STEAM perspective could develop Sweden’s education, research and innovation systems.

The conversation explores the difference between incremental improvements and radical innovation, how artistic methods strengthen the ability to handle uncertainty, and how new perspectives can be integrated without weakening technical excellence.

Afterwards, participants can join moderated round-table discussions in smaller groups with decision-makers from politics, academia and business.
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: Working together for safe medication management in municipal healthcare
content.description: How can municipal health and social care ensure safe and reliable medication treatment through greater collaboration between professions?
content.extendedDescription: Older people often have complex medication needs, while municipal healthcare faces a shortage of registered nurses and extensive delegation that puts patient safety at risk. Pharmacists can improve quality through medication reconciliation, training and support in mobile teams, relieving pressure on nurses and reducing errors. More and more municipalities are employing pharmacists, but the need is greater. Safe medication treatment requires the professions to work together and managers and decision-makers to prioritise expertise and collaboration. This panel discussion, organised by Sveriges Farmaceuter and Svensk Sjuksköterskeförening, highlights how cooperation can improve quality for older people.

content.title: How do we get more young people into education or employment?
content.description: Several municipalities are struggling with increasing numbers of young people who drop out of upper-secondary school and are neither working nor studying. Systems analyses help us better understand the causes and needs. Small-scale pilots support young people’s return to education and work, based on their own perspectives.
content.extendedDescription: When a young person falls outside education and employment, the step back can quickly become larger than it should be. Karlstads kommun has developed a deeper understanding through a systems analysis of young people covered by the municipal activity responsibility, KAA, and those who are neither working nor studying, UVAS. The findings clearly show that we need to act earlier, more intelligently and together. The municipality has therefore launched small-scale pilots testing new ways to support young people’s return to education and employment, starting from their own perspectives. In Almedalen, we want to share our experiences, inspire others and be inspired. We want to bring together more municipalities, public authorities and actors who wish to help shape future work against young people’s exclusion. We want to discuss solutions that are feasible, scalable and make a real difference in young people’s lives. How gaps between organisations arise, and how close collaboration between actors can reduce them. Always starting from what matters most: the young person’s perspective!
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: How do we encourage more young people to choose vocational education to meet Sweden’s skills needs?
content.description: How can Sweden take a thoughtful, long-term approach to helping more young people discover the potential of vocational education and thereby strengthen the future supply of skills? Can opportunities to try things out and gain experience spark an interest?
content.extendedDescription: In Karlstads kommun, initiatives such as vocational summer camps and structured guidance tailored to needs have generated curiosity and positive attitudes towards vocational programmes even before pupils choose upper-secondary education. During the summer holidays, younger children can try occupations in construction, electrical work, vehicles, technology and health and social care through practical activities and meetings with professionals. This increases interest and provides a better basis for future educational choices, strengthening both individual opportunities and society’s supply of skills. We want to discuss what is needed to help more young people make good choices, and how municipalities, politicians and industries can work together to scale up solutions that actually work. Many municipalities and industry organisations face the same challenge, but few have developed early interventions that reach the target group before upper-secondary choices are made. Questions include: how can early, practical encounters with occupations increase young people’s interest in vocational education? How can its status among young people be strengthened?

content.title: How can new approaches to SFI education strengthen the path to work and integration?
content.description: How can Swedish for Immigrants (SFI) develop so that more newcomers progress from language learning to work, further study and active participation in society? Which structures and interventions create sustainable paths to earning a living, and how can municipalities strengthen the link between SFI and the labour market?
content.extendedDescription: In this strategic conversation, we analyse the structures, models and interventions tailored to needs that can strengthen the transition from SFI to earning a living. Karlstads kommun has shifted SFI from a traditional focus on teaching materials towards more experience-based learning, with language practice in workplaces, work-related activities such as study visits and labour-market knowledge, and health-promoting approaches that strengthen both language and work capacity. Drawing on this and other examples, we discuss which changes and priorities could create more coherent and effective educational pathways nationally. content.title: Tactical upper-secondary choices — a threat to Sweden as an engineering nation?
content.description: Pupils who choose science or technology programmes at upper-secondary school receive lower final grades than comparable pupils on other university-preparatory programmes. When young people avoid science and technology programmes for tactical reasons, Sweden risks being weakened as an industrial nation.
content.extendedDescription: In December 2025, Sveriges Ingenjörer published the report “Taktikvalen till gymnasiet - Ett hot mot Sverige som ingenjörsnation”. Based on data from more than 200 000 pupils, it shows that pupils choosing science or technology programmes at upper-secondary school receive lower final grades than comparable pupils on other university-preparatory programmes. This leads many young people to avoid science and technology programmes, potentially weakening Sweden’s supply of skills and, with it, its ability to manage the green and digital transitions.
speakerTitles: National board member and education policy spokesperson
content.subject: Education
