content.title: Can we afford to train specialist nurses?
content.description: Specialist nursing education is critically important for healthcare to function. Higher education institutions across the country struggle to balance their budgets because of small student groups and eroded funding. There is also a shortage of clinical placements and qualified teachers.
content.extendedDescription:
The background is the well-known challenges facing this education nationally: financial problems and shortages of clinical placements and qualified teachers. The danger is that healthcare will not have the specialist nurses it needs, for example to carry out operations.

The seminar will discuss the findings of the inquiry “Samarbeten mellan lärosäten kring professionsutbildningar i hälso- och sjukvård”, conducted by Sveriges universitets- och högskoleförbund. We will also raise the question of some form of paid training employment for students on specialist nursing programmes. Another important issue is how to secure funding for this education, given the erosion of government funding for higher education in recent decades.
speakerTitles: Member of Parliament, Parliamentary Committee on Health and Welfare
content.subject: Education

content.title: How to attract the next generation to construction
content.description: Sweden faces major investments in housing, infrastructure and the green transition — but who will secure the skills? The construction industry offers stable jobs, career paths and innovation. Collaboration is now needed to make the industry a natural first choice.
content.extendedDescription:
The supply of skills in construction is a strategic issue for the entire economy. Municipalities and regions are planning for growth, businesses are investing in the green transition, and central government is driving major infrastructure projects. At the same time, a shortage of the right skills risks slowing progress.

Today, construction is far more than traditional craftsmanship. It involves digitalisation, sustainable materials, advanced logistics and project management in complex environments. It offers skilled roles, clear career paths and good opportunities for further training. For many, it is a stable route into employment; for others, a chance to grow as leaders and specialists.

The question is how we can jointly strengthen the match between education and the labour market, create attractive conditions and establish clear incentives in procurement and regulation. What is required of politicians, the education system and the industry itself to secure the skills and make construction a natural first choice?
content.subject: Construction

content.title: From innovation to patient benefit — Nordic perspectives on future healthcare
content.description: A global technology race in medicine and health is under way, and Europe risks falling behind. Meanwhile, the Nordic countries face an ageing population, growing care needs and skills shortages amid rapid technological development. How can Sweden accelerate the path from innovation to patient benefit by drawing on Nordic experience?
content.extendedDescription:
How can we shorten the time from research breakthroughs to clinical use? Leading actors from Sweden, Norway and Denmark come together to discuss how technology and medicine can develop in an integrated way, from research and testing environments to adoption in healthcare.

Using Nordic examples, we explore how collaboration between academia, healthcare and technology companies can be strengthened. What can Sweden learn from how our neighbours organise adoption, procurement and innovation partnerships? And what changes are needed to increase the pace and strengthen both patient benefits and competitiveness?

The programme is aimed at decision-makers and actors in healthcare, politics, academia and innovation systems.

The morning begins with breakfast networking from 8 before the stage programme starts. The seminar includes two panels with Nordic perspectives and ends with audience questions.

The organisers are the partners behind Chalmers Sahlgrenska Health Engineering Alliance.

content.title: The headteacher’s role in a storm of reforms — what happens to schools in 2028?
content.description: Sweden’s education system is undergoing reforms on a rarely seen scale. What will schools look like after 2028, and how do we ensure that headteachers have the authority and resources to implement the reforms?
content.extendedDescription:
Headteachers are in the middle of a storm of reforms. Their remit is rapidly growing in breadth and complexity, but the conditions are not keeping up.
The problem is not individual reforms, but the fact that so many are being implemented at once. The reforms risk failing if they cannot be put into practice.

A conversation about how headteachers can cope with the reform storm, and what the parties want to do to help schools fulfil their mission in the coming years.

Seminar from 8-9, followed by breakfast networking from 9-10.

content.title: The day after the election: what are the key challenges for Sweden’s energy sector, and how do we solve them?
content.description: Election campaigns are about what sounds good now, while energy systems must work for decades. After the election, reality remains: capacity shortages, delayed production and fragmented responsibility. What are we not talking about enough?
content.extendedDescription:
In today’s seminar, we tackle some of the uncomfortable paradoxes in the debate:
Why expand electricity generation and grids when demand is levelling off?
Who should pay for preparedness that everyone needs but few want to fund?
And how do we build an energy system quickly enough when uncertainty and hesitation shape decisions?

Preparedness, the conditions for electricity grids, returns and tariffs are raised not as technical details, but as choices for politics and society with major consequences.

Welcome to a conversation about energy issues that may determine Sweden’s future, despite barely determining the election.

content.title: High voltage: what the energy policy of the future looks like
content.description: Sweden can be a winner in the energy transition, but high energy prices and major investments are putting pressure on both industry and households. How do we secure competitiveness?
content.extendedDescription:
With its almost entirely fossil-free electricity system, strong companies and high climate ambitions, Sweden is well placed to benefit from the energy transition. Yet industry and households are under pressure from high energy prices, investment needs are extensive, and Europe’s priorities pull in different directions. How do we secure competitiveness, legitimacy and a long-term perspective in the transition?

This seminar brings together energy policy spokespersons from parliamentary parties and representatives of their youth organisations. Across political blocs and generations, we discuss the way forward. How can Sweden combine climate leadership with growth, jobs and stable energy prices?

Welcome to a debate about the future and how to make the transition competitive over the long term.

content.title: Import dependence or self-sufficiency? The energy system enables Sweden’s preparedness
content.description: Sweden has every opportunity to produce the fuels it needs in crisis and conflict, but we need the chance to make use of that potential. Regulations, infrastructure and policy instruments for circular solutions must now be designed to enable investment in domestic fuel production.
content.extendedDescription: We live in a time when the energy question has fundamentally changed. What just a few years ago was seen mainly as a climate and industrial issue is now also a security-policy reality. Sweden is a member of NATO. War is taking place in our neighbourhood. Total defence is being rebuilt. Trade routes are disrupted. Meanwhile, we still depend on imported fuels and global supply chains to keep transport, industry and essential services running. This raises a fundamental question: should Sweden be able to produce the energy and transport fuels needed in crisis and conflict itself, or should we depend on others? Today’s conversation addresses precisely this: what is needed to build national value chains for transport fuels, and the important role of the energy system in Sweden’s total defence, competitiveness and self-sufficiency.
speakerTitles: Head of electricity generation and society

content.title: How can entrepreneurship in upper-secondary school strengthen young people’s agency and confidence in the future?
content.description: Can entrepreneurship in upper-secondary school reduce inequality? Can running a business at school equip young people for life — as employees or entrepreneurs — by building confidence in the future?
content.extendedDescription:
Giving young people power over their future is more important than ever. Running a business through the UF entrepreneurship programme at upper-secondary school strengthens motivation for school and learning and builds self-confidence, while increasing young people’s employability and contributing to a sustainable supply of skills. By running UF businesses, pupils put their subject knowledge into practice and develop skills that are valuable whether they become employees or entrepreneurs.

Research shows that UF entrepreneurship develops entrepreneurial abilities among pupils on all programmes, particularly those with low academic confidence. It increases motivation at school, builds social skills and creates a more level playing field in the classroom.

In a panel discussion, representatives from business and education discuss how UF entrepreneurship serves as a practical resource for young people on their path towards working life. A dialogue-based session is followed by a reception and networking — a chance to strengthen young people’s opportunities together.

content.title: Policy is missing the climate targets — how can we turn things around in 180 weeks?
content.description: Electrifying Sweden’s vehicle fleet is crucial to meeting our climate targets. But the path ahead is still lined with myths and misconceptions that risk slowing progress.
content.extendedDescription:
In this discussion, we will demystify the most common beliefs standing in the way of the transition — and show what actually holds true.
Time is short: there are only 180 weeks left until Sweden’s 2030 targets. We must now separate fact from fiction and together create the momentum to take us all the way.

content.title: How do we build a more humane and resilient society — in Sweden and globally?
content.description: The world is at a decisive turning point. Authoritarian forces are strengthening their positions while fundamental international principles and international cooperation are being questioned. How do we build trust and stability in a time marked by uncertainty and division?
content.extendedDescription: Military spending is increasing while development aid is declining, despite growing humanitarian needs. Security is increasingly defined in terms of defence and border protection, while long-term stability is built through investment in human rights and conflict prevention. What role do Sweden’s development aid and foreign policies play in today’s security situation? Global Dialogue Garden is a meeting place in the heart of Almedalen where we discuss global issues and international solutions together with our partners. Here you can meet UN staff and representatives of civil society, business and academia for conversations about humanitarian needs, sustainable development and how we can jointly contribute to a more humane and resilient world. You are warmly invited to contribute to the dialogue.
content.subject: International affairs

content.title: Holding a steady course — leadership for a sustainable future
content.description: In a time of rapid change, political shifts and global challenges, it is easy to lose direction. How do you lead towards a future that people actually want to be part of? How do you stay true to your vision — and bring others with you — when the winds are blowing in every direction?
content.extendedDescription:
What kind of leadership is needed to drive a sustainable transition — in practice?

WIN WIN Award and Handelshögskolan vid Göteborgs universitet invite you to a conversation about how courage and responsibility can help tomorrow’s leaders stay on course in a time of rapid change.

We bring together leading experts to discuss the future, leadership, long-term thinking and sustainability — and what it takes to turn direction into concrete action. We also explore how narratives and strategies can unite people and organisations around a shared course towards a sustainable and inclusive future.
speakerTitles: Head of Sustainability Strategy and Policy
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: Does the national plan help or hinder Swedish growth?
content.description: Swedish businesses need functioning infrastructure to compete globally. Despite growing infrastructure budgets, capacity shortages and a maintenance backlog persist throughout the country. Does the national plan contribute to growth — or are new ways of making and financing decisions needed?
content.extendedDescription:
For Swedish businesses, from small entrepreneurs to large corporations, to grow and compete, they need infrastructure that is fit for purpose. Today, investment decisions are made through the national plan, with ever larger budgets for each period. At the same time, substantial maintenance backlogs and capacity shortages persist in metropolitan regions, industrial counties and export-intensive parts of the country.

Does the system meet Parliament’s transport policy objective of economically efficient and sustainable transport provision throughout the country over the long term? Does the model really contribute to Swedish growth and competitiveness — or should Sweden consider a different infrastructure planning model?

Business depends on long-term, reliable rules. During the seminar, we bring together companies and decision-makers to discuss whether the national plan is the right tool for the future — and what is needed to strengthen Sweden’s competitiveness through robust infrastructure decisions.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

content.title: What is research like when children and young people help create it?
content.description: What matters most when starting preschool class? What do young people need to feel well — and what should the local community do if young people decide? Children and young people’s right to express themselves on issues affecting them is now enshrined in law. But what is needed to move from hearing their voices to listening to them?
content.extendedDescription:
This seminar is for people conducting research or development work for children and young people who are considering how to do it WITH children and young people.

You will hear examples of what happens when young people co-create everything from research questions to methods, analysis and, yes, publication of the results. We describe what happens when young people present their own findings to decision-makers in their municipality on how to improve young people’s well-being.

The CHAP (Child Health and Parenting) research group at UU has formed a children’s panel consisting of six children aged 4-9. How does such a panel work? What can the children help with, how does it affect the research, and how do the children themselves experience their participation?

At this seminar, you will meet two researchers who have worked on co-created research with children and young people, and a professor who decided that children’s voices should not only be heard but also influence the knowledge we produce. Naturally, young people are taking part too.

content.title: Spaces for culture and people — needs before profit
content.description: How do we plan, prioritise and finance premises for schools, culture and places where people can meet? Today, many decisions about public environments are driven by economic efficiency, market thinking and short-term profitability. The question is what happens to the resources. Living and surviving are not all about money.
content.extendedDescription:
Physical environments affect working conditions, safety, participation and equality. When premises are adapted to budgets rather than the needs of the activities, the quality of teaching, cultural practice and social encounters risks deteriorating. This in turn affects democracy, because access to inclusive meeting places is a basic prerequisite for participation and influence.

The question is therefore not only economic, but also one of values and democracy.
What responsibility does society have to ensure that spaces for learning and culture are designed around people’s needs?
How is equity affected when resource allocation and the standard of premises differ between areas?
And what long-term costs to society arise when social sustainability gives way to short-term profitability?
Today, Anne-Charlotte works to bring grassroots perspectives all the way into the corridors of power — symbolically from the school floor to Grand Hôtel. She wants to highlight the needs of the people involved in these activities.

content.title: Bridges from Sweden out into the world
content.description: Today, we see increasing polarisation, loneliness and mistrust between generations and cultures. Without a historical perspective, people risk seeing identity as something static and restrictive, rather than living and shared. This can lead to fear of the unfamiliar. Innovations.
content.extendedDescription:
The societal issue we raise is how historical awareness and shared narratives can help build peaceful, cohesive societies in a time marked by division and conflicts over identity.

Looking back, we see how nations, cultures and people have long been intertwined. Relations between Spain and Sweden show how trade, migration, faith and ideas have built bridges across generations. History shows that societies develop through encounters and exchange — but also that conflicts arise when people forget their shared roots and instead reinforce differences. At the same time, role models such as Dagny Carlsson show how a perspective on life spanning generations can create hope, curiosity and confidence in the future. In a conversation about visions of a place where innovation, peace and joy can meet, we talk with the guests concerned about the importance of courage.

Creating a “peace story” therefore means actively using history to understand our own time, rather than romanticising it.

content.description: How can you, as a young person, make your voice heard above the noise of adults? How can you have the opportunity to share your thoughts on important issues such as our present and future?
content.extendedDescription:
In 2022, Bbeabridge launched the What about Youth Voice initiative with a simple but important idea: to give young people a real opportunity to be heard. In a time marked by rapidly growing societal challenges, young people often live closest to the future — yet, paradoxically, they are rarely allowed to help shape it.

Despite limited resources, What about Youth Voice continued to develop as a forum for dialogue, reflection and shared responsibility. Now, a few years later, Bbeabridge sees an even greater need to listen. Society is changing rapidly — technologically, socially and politically — and young people’s perspectives are more important than ever.

Youth Voice is therefore taking a new step. Bbeabridge has made it a central task to collect young people’s thoughts, ideas and visions around three crucial questions about the future: what worries young people most today? What gives them hope? And what changes do they themselves want to see in society?

Between the interviews, Charlotte Wihk will play music and bring joy.

content.title: How can young people’s voices be heard above the noise of adults?
content.description: How can you, as a young person, make your voice heard above the noise of adults? How can you have the opportunity to share your thoughts on important issues such as our present and future?
content.extendedDescription:
In 2022, Bbeabridge launched the What about Youth Voice initiative with a simple but important idea: to give young people a real opportunity to be heard. In a time marked by rapidly growing societal challenges, young people often live closest to the future — yet, paradoxically, they are rarely allowed to help shape it.

Despite limited resources, What about Youth Voice continued to develop as a forum for dialogue, reflection and shared responsibility. Now, a few years later, Bbeabridge sees an even greater need to listen. Society is changing rapidly — technologically, socially and politically — and young people’s perspectives are more important than ever.

Youth Voice is therefore taking a new step. Bbeabridge has made it a central task to collect young people’s thoughts, ideas and visions around three crucial questions about the future: what worries young people most today? What gives them hope? And what changes do they themselves want to see in society?

Between the interviews, Charlotte Wihk will play music and bring joy.

content.title: Out into nature, into community — health as a bridge builder
content.description: Prioritising community and health should be seen as a public good. Exercising together in nature is important for everyone. Having access to environments that promote physical and mental health matters. This includes green spaces and meeting places with nature and culture for young and old alike.
content.extendedDescription:
As urbanisation increases, natural areas risk becoming scarce. Spending time in nature promotes health and brings many benefits: less muscle tension, reduced stress levels and a stronger immune system.

Humans have lived in nature for most of our evolutionary history, so it is hardly surprising that spending time there makes us feel good — something research also confirms. It is therefore important to build bridges between different environments so that everyone can engage in varied physical activity and outdoor recreation in safe, accessible settings close to nature. Loneliness and sedentary lifestyles are growing public health problems. Environments designed without considering encounters, accessibility and activity risk reinforcing isolation and inactivity, and particularly exclusion in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas. This is a societal issue we want to highlight: a pair of walking poles, friends, or perhaps an exercise group. We are building bridges to Englagård, which has a working farm.

content.description: Why are brain training and social stimulation often regarded as optional leisure interests rather than part of preventive public health work? content.extendedDescription:
Ageism. Should older people be seen as an asset, active and involved in society’s continuing development?

Investing in the interplay between brain and body means strengthening people’s autonomy and quality of life and making use of their accumulated knowledge, experience and more.

Do we see cognitive health as a private matter, or as a shared resource for society worth promoting? Building bridges between generations has always been necessary throughout history and strengthens people’s sense of connection and trust in one another. content.title: How can writing and art build a bridge to community?
content.description: The central question concerns value. Why is culture often seen as consumption rather than social infrastructure? Creative projects bringing people together around a place or shared theme show how narratives shape our sense of belonging. Images become important.
content.extendedDescription:
The societal issue raised is the role of culture and creativity in creating cohesion, participation and a shared identity in a time marked by polarisation and social fragmentation. How can art and writing serve as tools for bringing people together across social, geographical and generational boundaries?

In many public debates, culture is regarded as secondary — a “soft” sector that can be deprioritised when resources are limited. Yet experience and research show that artistic expression strengthens people’s ability to understand themselves and one another. When people create, interpret and share narratives, shared frames of reference emerge. This builds trust, a fundamental prerequisite for democracy. The question matters because a lack of shared narratives can reinforce feelings of exclusion. When people do not feel that their perspectives fit within society’s narrative, the distance between groups risks growing. Our guest is Soledad Bellange, art…

content.title: 2.5 million encounters on Quora — questions and answers as bridge builders
content.description: The courage to join the global conversation and the importance of making room in public debate for experiences from everyday life. At a time when public discussion is often dominated by established voices, Quora allows any question to be asked and anyone to write an answer.
content.extendedDescription:
A democratic challenge: whose experiences count, and which perspectives risk being silenced?

Not being afraid to enter public debate is fundamentally a matter of democracy. If people with experience from the “ground level” — schools, healthcare, culture and civil society — do not take part in the conversation, decision-making risks becoming detached from reality. As the distance between decision-making rooms and everyday life grows, trust declines.

The problem is that public debate can feel exclusionary. It often requires access to platforms, networks and confidence in expressing oneself. Digital forums and podcasts have opened new opportunities, but they also bring a harsher tone and greater polarisation. This may make many people hesitate to take part, even though their perspectives are needed. The societal issue therefore matters because it concerns the practical conditions for freedom of expression. Having the right to speak is not enough — people must also feel that it is possible. Soledad Bellange joins us to discuss the importance of diplomacy.

content.title: Building bridges and a sense of coherence — a path towards lasting peace
content.description: When people do not feel understood, included or meaningfully engaged, they risk becoming excluded. This not only creates social divides but also undermines long-term peace and stability.
content.extendedDescription:
The societal issue is how a sense of coherence (KASAM) can provide a foundation for preventing social isolation, polarisation and conflict. In today’s society, many people experience a lack of participation, comprehensibility and meaningfulness — three central components of KASAM. This affects both individuals’ mental health and society’s social cohesion.

A dialogue also attended by peacemaker Börje Erdtman, a man who has inspired others and achieved peace. The question therefore matters: how do we build societies that strengthen people’s sense of coherence while creating social bridges between groups? Building bridges is about more than physical infrastructure or symbolic encounters; it means creating real structures and relationships that enable people to understand, influence and find meaning in their everyday lives and in society.

When societies lack such structures, conflicts risk escalating, marginalisation increasing and democratic participation weakening. KASAM and building bridges = right.

content.title: Bridge builders, oral health and social responsibility
content.description: Is oral health part of society’s responsibility? Is oral health also part of the body? Folktandvården in Region Stockholm has decided to stop offering subscription dental care agreements to people turning 67 or older. The decision means that no new agreements are signed.
content.extendedDescription:
What does this mean?

Better general health through good oral health!
It is well known that oral health affects the health of the whole body. Many studies on the subject point, among other things, to the link between bacteria in the mouth and cardiovascular disease.

That bacteria from the mouth can spread and affect other organs is nothing new, but not everyone may know that a toothbrush is also a major breeding ground for bacteria. Magnus Nylander, who holds a doctorate in medical science, writes in Medicinsk Access about toothbrushes and the importance of keeping them clean. He writes that a toothbrush can become like a “dirty dishcloth” full of living bacteria from both the mouth and the bathroom. A toothbrush can cause gastroenteritis and reinfect the body after courses of antibiotics. Rinsing a toothbrush is not enough: in a damp environment, it can take several days for it to dry and for the bacteria to disappear.
Dr Magnus Nylander, nutrition researcher and dentist.
Time permitting, we will also discuss new ways of thinking about membership in associations. Multiple membership is one solution.

content.title: How can we move from opponents to partners in an increasingly polarised society?
content.description: One of the greatest societal problems of our time is when people and groups see each other as opponents rather than partners. This creates conflicts that make it harder to find solutions to everything from climate change to social security and global development.
content.extendedDescription:
The societal issue raised is the role of culture and creativity in creating cohesion, participation and a shared identity in a time marked by polarisation and social fragmentation. How can art and writing serve as tools for bringing people together across social, geographical and generational boundaries?

In many public debates, culture is regarded as secondary — a “soft” sector that can be deprioritised when resources are limited. Yet experience and research show that artistic expression strengthens people’s ability to understand themselves and one another. When people create, interpret and share narratives, shared frames of reference emerge. This builds trust, a fundamental prerequisite for democracy.
The question matters because a lack of shared narratives can reinforce feelings of exclusion. When people do not feel that their perspectives fit within society’s narrative, the distance between groups risks growing. Creativity can work well.
